results.name: four_minus_two_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate on 4-example sets minus yes rate on 2-example sets; observed above the model mean means people generalize more (not less) with more examples than the size principle predicts.
results.code:
# name: four_minus_two_example_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate on 4-example sets minus yes rate on 2-example sets; observed above the model mean means people generalize more (not less) with more examples than the size principle predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    E = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:4]
        E[i, :len(v)] = v
    X = E[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN padded
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    a = r[n == 4]; b = r[n == 2]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: yes_rate_parity_violation
results.description: Among sets whose examples all share one parity, the yes rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed above the model's mean means people generalize across parity more than the odd/even rules allow.
results.code:

def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    E = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:4]
        E[i, :len(v)] = v
    X = E[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN padded
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)

    m = (lo == hi) & ((t % 2) != lo)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: sd_of_set_mean_yes_rate
results.description: Standard deviation across example sets (with >=10 responses) of each set's mean yes rate; observed below the model mean means the model differentiates sets (broad vs narrow concepts) more sharply than people do.

    E = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):

        E[i, :len(v)] = v

results.name: distance_rating_correlation
results.description: Pearson correlation between yes and log(1+distance from target to nearest example), among targets not in the set; more negative observed than model means people show stronger numerical-similarity gradients than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: distance_rating_correlation
# description: Pearson correlation between yes and log(1+distance from target to nearest example), among targets not in the set; more negative observed than model means people show stronger numerical-similarity gradients than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    E = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:4]
        E[i, :len(v)] = v
    X = E[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN padded
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    d = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = d > 0
    a = np.log1p(d[m]); b = r[m]
    if a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1])

results.name: yes_rate_far_outside_range
results.description: Yes rate for targets outside the [min,max] span of the examples and more than 20 from every example; observed above the model mean means people say yes to remote numbers more than the model (missing response noise or broader generalization).
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_far_outside_range
# description: Yes rate for targets outside the [min,max] span of the examples and more than 20 from every example; observed above the model mean means people say yes to remote numbers more than the model (missing response noise or broader generalization).
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    E = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:4]
        E[i, :len(v)] = v
    X = E[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN padded
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)

    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate in the second half of trials (trial_index >= median) minus the first half; a value different from the model mean (which has no time dependence) means responding drifts over the session (e.g. becoming more conservative).
results.code:
# name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate in the second half of trials (trial_index >= median) minus the first half; a value different from the model mean (which has no time dependence) means responding drifts over the session (e.g. becoming more conservative).
def test_statistic(df):
    codes, uniq = pd.factorize(df["number_set"].astype(str))
    E = np.full((len(uniq), 4), np.nan)
    for i, s in enumerate(uniq):
        v = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")][:4]
        E[i, :len(v)] = v
    X = E[codes]  # (rows, 4) examples, NaN padded
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    late = ti >= np.median(ti)
    if late.all() or (~late).all():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[late].mean() - r[~late].mean())
